title: No Rescue for a Besieged City
overview: With Babylon's army at the walls, King Zedekiah hopes for a miracle, but Jeremiah answers that the city will fall and that surrender is the only way to survive.

parts.label: The king asks for a miracle (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Around 588 BC Babylon's army surrounded Jerusalem, and King Zedekiah sent a priest and an official (a different Pashhur from the one in the previous chapter) to ask Jeremiah to consult the LORD. He hoped for a rescue like the one a century earlier, when an Assyrian army besieging the city suddenly withdrew.

parts.label: God will fight against them (vv. 3-7)
parts.note: The answer turns the old rescue stories upside down: the God who once fought for Israel with an outstretched hand now says he will fight against the city, so its weapons will be useless and disease, hunger and the sword will follow. Later chapters and 2 Kings report that Babylon killed Zedekiah's sons in front of him, then blinded him and took him to Babylon.

parts.label: A choice of life or death (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: Echoing the old choice between life and death in Deuteronomy, Jeremiah tells ordinary people that staying means death, while surrendering to Babylon means escaping with nothing but their lives. Urging surrender in wartime sounded like treason, and Jeremiah was later imprisoned for it.

parts.label: A charge to the royal family (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: The royal family, descended from David, is told to give fair judgments promptly, in the morning when courts usually met, and to rescue people who have been robbed. Their own wrongdoing, not just Babylon's power, is named as the reason for the coming fire.

parts.label: The proud city on the rock (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: Jerusalem sat on high rocky ground ringed by valleys, so its people boasted that nobody could break in. The forest set on fire probably pictures the city's many buildings made of cedar wood, though the exact image is uncertain.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to read God saying he will fight against the city: some take it as God directly bringing the destruction, others as God withdrawing protection and letting the results of injustice and political choices run their course.
think: When trouble comes, why might it feel easier to ask for rescue than to ask what might need to change?
